These young individuals occupy shallow nursery habitats such as estuaries and mangrove-lined creeks, where predation risk is reduced and prey densities are high. The relatively advanced developmental state at birth, evidenced by a fully formed rostrum with functional teeth, suggests a strategy of precocial independence from maternal provisioning shortly after emergence. Available records indicate that births occur predominantly during the warmer months, aligning with the temperature range at which these data were originally collected. The neonatal length at birth has been corroborated across multiple field surveys in Florida Bay and the Gulf of Mexico, lending confidence to this baseline measurement for early life history modeling.

Corresponding to this formidable body size, the maximum recorded adult wet weight is approximately 350,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 350,000 grams], a mass that underscores the substantial somatic investment required to sustain such a large, slow-growing elasmobranch. The ultimate total length value serves as a critical benchmark for evaluating population recovery targets.

This longevity estimate, originally derived from studies of the congener Pristis perotteti, aligns with known age-at-length relationships for P. pectinata and is consistent with the slow maturation rates typical of large-bodied elasmobranchs. A long reproductive window is further supported by the species' delayed age at first breeding, which field data place at approximately 6.2 years [tR = approximately 6.2 years] when water temperatures average 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This protracted pre-reproductive phase likely reflects the time needed to accumulate sufficient body reserves and attain the structural size necessary for successful gestation. The combination of late maturity and extended lifespan positions P. pectinata as a k-selected species with low natural replacement potential.

Climate-driven shifts in coastal water temperatures could therefore have pronounced effects on population recruitment dynamics.

From a conservation physiology perspective, the life history parameters of Pristis pectinata reveal a species acutely vulnerable to anthropogenic mortality. The combination of late age at first breeding, low fecundity per event, and slow growth creates a demographic lag that impedes rapid population recovery after declines. By contrast, the large ultimate body size and correspondingly high asymptotic mass may confer some resilience to periodic environmental stressors, as larger individuals can buffer against short-term resource shortages. Continued monitoring of length at birth across nurseries provides a sensitive indicator of maternal condition and habitat quality. Comparative studies with the largetooth sawfish Pristis pristis indicate broadly similar life history strategies, though P. pectinata appears to reach pubertal length at a slightly smaller size, suggesting subtle differences in growth allocation between the two sister species.
